definition: Replicable means able to be repeated by others with the same results.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word replicable. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know replicable should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The safety training proved replicable: any branch that followed its nine written steps saw the same drop in accidents.
A suggestive result hints that something real is there — once, in one place; replicable is the rank above it, earned only when strangers rerun the recipe and the same answer comes back.
Settled outruns replicable: a replicable finding repeats whenever strangers rerun it, while a settled one has repeated so often it lives in the textbooks.

Repeatable says the same hands can do it again — the same lab, the same kitchen, the same result tomorrow. Replicable raises the bar to strangers: hand the written method to a team that has never seen it, and the result still comes back. Every replicable method is repeatable; the reverse can fail.

Reproducible is the report-checker's word: take the original data and analysis, rerun them, and the same numbers fall out. Replicable makes the bolder claim — a fresh team, fresh materials, only the written recipe, and still the same finding. Reproducible re-checks the arithmetic; replicable re-runs the world.

Replicable is the difference between a feat and a method.
A feat happens once and gathers legends; a method can be handed to a stranger and turn out the same result on demand.
The word doesn't promise the result is good — only that it repeats, which is why laboratories, kitchens, and coaching staffs prize it equally.
Replicable is the working scientist's seal: hand a stranger the recipe and the result comes back again.
It pairs with its unit-mates falsifiable — testable at all — and tenable — still defensible after the test.
A replicable recipe is a method; an unrepeatable one is a story.

When a small materials lab announced a battery that charged in ninety seconds, headlines arrived within hours; belief took longer.
The field had been burned before by dramatic results that no one else could ever produce again.
So the lab did something unusual: it published every step -- the powder grinding times, the oven temperatures, even the brand of foil.
Within a season, teams in Seoul, Zurich, and Austin had built the cell from the instructions alone and matched the ninety-second charge.
Only then did the journals stop calling the result a curiosity and start calling it replicable, and the review that mattered was written by strangers.
